idiom_name: case class with default parameters and named arguments + copy (stdlib mutable.Builder for collections)
implementation_notes: Scala gives the call site what the builder simulates: parameters can declare defaults and be passed by name in any order (Server(host = "db", maxConns = 10)), and copy derives a variant of an existing value - Bloch calls this out explicitly when motivating the Java builder. The standard library also ships a literal builder abstraction for collections (scala.collection.mutable.Builder with += and result(), plus BuildFrom/Factory since 2.13), which is what generic code uses to accumulate elements without knowing the concrete collection type. A hand-written fluent builder is justified when construction performs effects (I/O, resource acquisition) or when an external driver must assemble the product step by step.
code_sketch:
final case class Server(host: String, port: Int = 8080, maxConns: Int = 100)

val a = Server(host = "db")                    // named + defaulted
val b = a.copy(maxConns = 10)                  // variant of an instance

val xs: List[Int] = {                          // scala.collection.Builder
  val builder = List.newBuilder[Int]
  (1 to 3).foreach(builder += _)
  builder.result()
}
pitfalls: copy is shallow: collection and array members are shared with the copy unless they are copied explicitly.
Builders are not reusable or thread-safe: except for ReusableBuilder a builder must not be touched after result(), and sharing one across futures silently corrupts the collection.
Default parameter values apply only when the argument is omitted, so passing null (easy from Java APIs) is accepted by the compiler and fails later.
